name: PT Bank Oke Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Oke Indonesia: a real book, not enough earnings power
frontmatter.summary: A capital-rich Korean-controlled micro-bank earning a mid-single-digit ROE against a double-digit cost of equity. The shares look cheap on book but are not cheap on earnings power: we initiate at SELL with a target of Rp45.
thesis: The balance sheet is genuine and over-capitalised: 42.2% CAR and a 0.42 price-to-book, but the capital earns a fraction of what it costs to hold.
Sustainable ROE is capped near the mid-single digits by a 5.7% NIM, a 60.0% cost-to-income ratio and credit costs that must normalise from an unusually low FY2025 charge.
Funding is the binding constraint: loans are 119.5% of deposits against a system LDR of 88.1%, so growth must be funded by costly deposits or borrowings, not by a CASA franchise.
The 7.5% free float, against the exchange's 15.0% minimum, is an overhang and a governance discount, not a catalyst we are paid to underwrite.
The market appears to price a materially higher sustainable ROE than the bank has ever earned; our warranted value is Rp45 and the risk-reward is negative.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: whether the near-zero 2026 provisioning charge holds or is trued up in Q4
Bank Indonesia board meeting: a hike toward {{fact.F24|pctv}} would pressure the deposit-heavy funding base
Annual general meeting: any capital-return or free-float remedy after another year of retained earnings

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bank Oke Indonesia Tbk (DNAR.JK) at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp45**, implying a return of **-55.1%** from the last traded price of Rp100. The target is the probability-weighted value across our scenarios after the house liquidity discount of 20% that we apply to a stock with a 7.5% free float and three-month average daily turnover of IDR140.2m [S0]. This is a fundamental call, not a trading one: the shares are illiquid enough that entry and exit are themselves part of the thesis.

The bank is not a broken institution. It has a real franchise in Indonesian corporate and retail lending and one of the strongest capital ratios in the listed sector at 42.2% [S16]. It earned IDR160.0bn in FY2025, a threefold increase, on company-disclosed net interest income of IDR688.9bn [S16]. The problem is what that capital earns. FY2025 ROE was 4.3% [S16], and our through-cycle build reaches only the mid-single digits. Against a cost of equity of 11.9% — the engine's build, set out in the valuation section — the economic spread is negative. A bank that earns below its cost of equity is worth less than its book, and the question is only how much less. We cannot vouch for the loan book: the company's NPL, LAR and coverage ratios are not in any source we could archive, and we do not assume they are clean.

The market disagrees, or at least prices the shares at 0.42 times FY2026E book [S0]. Work the identity backwards — implied sustainable ROE equals the P/BV multiple times the spread between the cost of equity and terminal growth, plus that growth — and today's 0.42 multiple, a 11.9% cost of equity and 3.0% growth require a sustained return close to two and a half points above the 4.3% the bank earned in FY2025. Our warranted P/BV is 0.22x on a sustainable ROE of 4.9%, which produces Rp51. The residual-income cross-check is harsher at Rp45 because it charges the cost of equity against a growing equity base year by year, so it is the lower of the two methods. Blending the two gives a fundamental value of Rp45.

Three things could change the view. First, a genuine capital-return policy: with 42.2% CAR and a 0.4x multiple, a buyback or a special dividend would transfer value from the balance sheet to shareholders and could close part of the gap. Second, a faster-than-expected normalisation of the loan book toward higher-yielding, better-priced corporate assets without a matching rise in credit cost. Third, a sale of control: a bank with 91.4% insider ownership, a listed shell and a tiny float is a plausible acquisition or delisting candidate, and that option value is not in our fundamental number. We take the first two seriously and the third as a bull-case kicker, but none of them is the base case.

What the market is paid for today is the hope of a re-rating. What it owns is a sub-scale lender whose deposits cost more than its peers', whose fee income is effectively nil, and whose profits in the last two years have been flattered by unusually low provisioning. That is a poor combination at a premium to our warranted value.

Bank Oke Indonesia sits in the smallest tier of Indonesian commercial banks. Institutions of this size typically lack the deposit franchise and the fee businesses of the large banks, so their returns depend almost entirely on spread income and cost discipline. In a system where the largest banks earn mid-teens to high-teens ROE, the small-bank tier has structurally lower returns and trades at a discount to book much of the time. That is context, not a source for any figure.

PT Bank Oke Indonesia Tbk is an Indonesian commercial bank headquartered in Central Jakarta. It was founded in 1990, merged with Bank Oke Indonesia in 2018 and adopted the OK Bank brand in 2019 [S0][S6]. It takes savings and time deposits and lends through current-account, working-capital, investment, lines-of-credit, unsecured and payroll products, and offers mobile banking and safe-deposit services [S0]. Its operating footprint covers DKI Jakarta, Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java and Bali [S16]. It employed 317 people at the last count [S0].

The business is, in substance, a monoline spread lender. The company reports net interest income of IDR688.9bn for FY2025 [S16]; the data pack's interest line is IDR705.8bn, which is interest income less interest expense on the pack's own presentation, and non-interest income was IDR5.3bn, a rounding error against the interest book [S0]. Adding the pack's two components gives total operating income of IDR711.1bn [S0]. There is no meaningful wealth, treasury, insurance or transaction-fee engine to cushion a margin squeeze. That matters for the valuation: the bank has one lever, the spread, and one shock absorber, cost.

The loan book was IDR10,730.0bn at the end of FY2025, up from IDR9,300.0bn a year earlier, a growth rate well above system credit growth [S16][S22]. Deposits were IDR8,980.0bn against IDR7,540.0bn in FY2024 [S16]. Because loans exceed deposits, the balance sheet is funded partly by borrowings and equity: the loan-to-deposit ratio is 119.5% [S0][S16]. That is the single most important operating fact about this bank. Indonesian banks on average lend about 88.1% of their deposits [S22]; OK Bank lends nearly a third more than it collects. The gap is bridged by wholesale funding, which is more expensive and more cyclical than a retail deposit base.

Strategy, as presented at the May 2026 public expose, is to strengthen the asset base before growing it: improve borrower quality, expand retail and corporate credit selectively, diversify products, optimise the branch network, strengthen risk management and improve operating efficiency. On the liability side the explicit priority is a higher CASA share, supported by digital channels and a wider customer base [S16][S19]. Management also points to digital transformation and technology-based services as the route to cost efficiency [S16]. The compliance director told the press in July 2026 that the funding strategy is focused on savings and current accounts, with selective credit growth supported by adequate liquidity [S19].

The controlling shareholder is Korean. A 2022 rights issue was absorbed by APRO Financial Co Ltd, which was reported at the time as taking its stake to just over ninety percent and injecting new capital at an exercise price far above today's market [S2]. The data pack now names OK Next Co Ltd as the parent [S0]. We could not retrieve a current annual report to reconcile the two, and we flag that as an evidence gap rather than paper over it. What is not in doubt is the concentration: insiders hold 91.4% of the shares and institutions hold 0.0%, leaving a free float of 7.5% [S0]. The bank is a controlled subsidiary in listed form, and minority holders have correspondingly little influence over capital allocation.

Competitively, OK Bank is a challenger with no scale advantage. It is sub-scale against the system, has no national deposit franchise and competes for corporate loans against banks with cheaper funding and deeper relationships. Its differentiator is a Korean shareholder and, historically, access to Korean-linked corporate borrowers; management has said the focus is domestic corporate business rather than reliance on Korean companies [S19]. That is a sensible diversification, but it also means the bank is competing head-on with larger domestic banks in exactly the corporate segment that is growing fastest and where pricing power sits with the strongest franchises [S22].

A listed subsidiary with a free float below the exchange's minimum is a recurring feature of the Indonesian small-cap market. Such companies often remain listed for the visibility and the licence rather than for equity capital, and minority shareholders frequently have no path to control or to a liquidity event. We treat the structure as a discount factor rather than as an automatic catalyst.

The Indonesian banking system is growing credit faster than deposits. System loans reached 13.3 percent growth in September 2026, on a stock of IDR9,245.1tn, while third-party funds grew 8.2% to IDR10,492.2tn [S22][S18]. The composition matters more than the aggregate for OK Bank. Corporate credit grew 21.3% and investment credit grew faster still, while working capital grew 11.9% and consumer credit only 4.9% [S22]. Current accounts were the fastest-growing deposit category at 12.6%, with savings ahead of time deposits [S18]. In other words, the system's growth is concentrated in exactly the two areas OK Bank says it wants: corporate lending and CASA gathering.

Asset quality looks contained at the system level. Gross NPL was 2.1% and net NPL 0.8% in September 2026, with a loan-at-risk ratio of 8.5% [S22]. Capital is plentiful at 24.3% and system liquidity is adequate, with an LDR of 88.1% [S22]. This is a supportive backdrop for a small bank that needs to grow into its capital. It is also a backdrop in which credit competition is intense, because every bank has capital and liquidity and wants the same corporate assets.

The rate cycle is the swing factor for margins. The house macro deck carries a BI rate of 5.8% and holds it there through FY2027E, so our base case assumes no policy-rate move; the risk is on the other side, with market economists projecting a rise toward 6.2% by the end of 2026 to defend the rupiah [S20]. For a bank funded largely by time deposits and wholesale money, a hike passes through to cost of funds faster than it reprices the asset book, especially if the loan book is corporate and fixed-rate at origination. That is a risk we carry in the bear case, not a base-case assumption. OK Bank's disclosed NIM of 5.7% in FY2025 [S16] is high by system standards, which is flattering at the top of a cycle and vulnerable on the way down. Measured on the template's average-total-assets denominator the margin is 5.9%, and our base case gives back only a sliver to 5.7% by FY2030E.

Regulation cuts both ways. The exchange's 15.0% free-float minimum is the most immediate structural rule for this name [S24]; with 7.5% float, the company is a candidate for a rights issue, a sell-down or, at the limit, a delisting process [S0]. Prudential rules are not the constraint: 42.2% CAR is far above any regulatory minimum [S16]. The government's subsidised credit programmes are expanding, but the main channels are the state banks, not a Korean-controlled smallest-tier lender, so the subsidised-credit boom visible in the news flow is not a direct tailwind for OK Bank.

The competitive picture is weak on every axis we test. Rivalry is high because the system is liquid and corporate borrowers have many lenders. Buyer power is high for the same reason. Supplier power — the depositor — is high because OK Bank has no CASA franchise and must pay for term money. New entrants are a real threat in retail and SME digital lending, where the bank's own digital push is defensive rather than disruptive. Substitutes are moderate: capital markets and fintech take some corporate and consumer demand but not the core working-capital relationship. The moat, in honest terms, is a licence and a controlling shareholder's capital, not a franchise. That is why we value the bank on residual income and warranted book rather than on a growth multiple [S22].

Five-forces analysis for small banks in emerging markets usually turns on funding. A bank with a cheap deposit franchise can survive mediocre asset pricing; a bank without one is a price-taker on both sides of the balance sheet. This is the standard lens we apply, not a company-specific claim.

The historical record is one of a small bank growing its balance sheet faster than its profit. Total assets rose from IDR11,075.2bn in FY2023 to IDR11,870.5bn and IDR13,417.6bn in FY2025, while net profit went from IDR28.7bn to IDR50.0bn and IDR160.0bn [S0][S16]. The FY2025 jump is the number that needs explaining, and the explanation is not a step-change in the franchise.

Net interest income grew to IDR688.9bn in FY2025 from IDR615.2bn on the pack's basis, and the company-disclosed margin was 5.7% [S16]. The second is the filed number and the first is the pack's, and they do not agree: the pack's interest line is IDR705.8bn for FY2025 because it subtracts interest expense from interest income without the LK's netting of fee-based interest, a difference of roughly a fortieth of net interest income [S0][S16]. We use the disclosed figure in the narrative and flag the pack line as a presentation difference, not a restatement of profit: net profit, equity and ROE are unaffected, so neither the history nor the valuation moves with it.

That accounts for part of the profit increase. The rest comes from provisioning. On our reconstruction, FY2024 carried an implied credit charge near two percent of loans, while FY2025 carried well below one percent [S0]. When a bank's provision charge falls by more than a percentage point of loans, profit can triple without anything improving in the underlying business. That is the correct lens on FY2025: it was a normalisation year, not a new earnings level.

The nine months to September 2026 continue the pattern. Profit for the period already exceeds the whole of FY2025, with the margin running near 5.9% on average total assets and provisions close to nil [S0]. A bank cannot run at a zero cost of risk indefinitely; either the charge normalises or the loan book is not being marked honestly. We therefore forecast a FY2026 credit cost of 0.5% — enough for a Q4 catch-up on the near-zero nine-month charge — rising to 1.1% in FY2028E and 1.2% long run. This is the single assumption that drives the difference between our forecast and the extrapolation of 2026.

On the revenue side we build from the observed lending rate, not from guidance. Loans were IDR10,810.0bn in May 2026, up 12.7% year on year [S19], after IDR10,730.0bn at December 2025 against IDR9,300.0bn in FY2024 [S16]. We therefore model loan growth of 12.5% in FY2026E, in line with the latest actual and with system credit growth of 13.3% [S22]. The five-month move from December 2025 to May 2026 was barely positive, but that stub is a seasonal artefact of deposit run-off in the first half, not a break in the year-on-year trend, and we do not annualise it. Growth then steps down to 12.0% and settles at 10.0% because the loan-to-deposit ratio ties lending to deposit gathering. Deposits grow 14.0% in FY2026E — more than in FY2025 on our numbers, and enough to keep ahead of loans — so the LDR eases from 119.5% to 117.9% and then to 116.4%, still far above the system [S22]. The margin holds at 5.9%, the annualised nine-month run-rate on average total assets, and gives back only a sliver to 5.7% as system deposit growth of 8.2% trails credit growth and the bank pays up for term money [S22]; there is no policy-rate compression because the house deck holds BI flat [S20]. Cost-to-income is held near 60.0%, in line with our reconstruction of FY2025, and drifts only modestly lower as digital channels scale.

The net interest income bridge follows directly from those two lines. Earning assets — total assets, the denominator this template and its NIM input share — go from IDR13,420.0bn to IDR15,089.1bn, and the margin holds at 5.9%, which takes net interest income from the filed IDR688.9bn to IDR833.9bn. There is no third denominator in the model: the multiple of loans, the assets and the margin are all measured on the same basis, so the forecast can be rebuilt from the two inputs without a reconciling item [S16][S0].

The resulting path is unexciting by design. Net profit is IDR209.4bn in FY2026E, then IDR193.9bn as the credit charge normalises, before grinding up to IDR236.2bn. EPS is Rp12 and book value per share rises from Rp225 to Rp287. ROE rises from the FY2025 actual of 4.3% to 5.4% in the normalisation year, then falls back to the mid-four-percent range as provisioning normalises, before reaching 5.0% on a larger NII base. The FY2026E step is not a forecast of a better franchise: it is the arithmetic of a 5.9% margin on a balance sheet that grew 12.5% against a near-zero provision charge, and it reverses as soon as the charge is marked at a through-cycle level. That is the honest earnings power of the franchise: the capital is growing, but the return on it is not [S0].

Capital and funding are the two balance-sheet stories. The estimated capital ratio falls from 39.5% to 31.6% as loans grow faster than retained earnings, still comfortably above requirements. The bank pays no dividend in any year of the data history [S0], so all earnings are retained and the capital cushion stays large. That is prudent but value-destructive when the marginal return on equity is below the cost of equity: every retained rupiah is reinvested at a negative spread. Funding is the offsetting risk. With an LDR of 119.5%, the bank depends on wholesale and interbank money, and a deposit slowdown would force it to slow lending or pay up for funds — the classic small-bank squeeze.

Earnings-quality flags, in the order they matter. First, the provision charge: FY2025 and 2026 profits are flattered by a credit charge well below the through-cycle level, so headline growth overstates the franchise [S0]. Second, revenue concentration: non-interest income is negligible, so there is no fee cushion and no diversification benefit [S0]. Third, related-party opacity: the controlling shareholder is a Korean financial group, and we could not obtain a current annual report to quantify related-party lending or funding; we treat this as an unquantified governance discount rather than assume it away [S2][S0]. Fourth, disclosure: the FY2025 audit opinion and the auditor's identity could not be verified from the sources available to us, because the company's investor-relations site is script-rendered and its annual-report PDFs were not retrievable. We flag the gap and do not claim a clean bill of health. Fifth, structure: the October 2025 cancellation of treasury shares reduced the share count to 16,892 million [S3]; the action is benign in itself but it raises the insider percentage and worsens the free-float position.

The accruals screen is not meaningful for a bank; we use the provisioning trend instead, and it is the clearest warning in the model. On the data pack, operating cash flow swung from a large inflow in FY2023 to an outflow in FY2025 [S0], which for a bank mostly reflects deposit and loan flows rather than earnings quality. The provisioning path is the signal, and it says the last two years of profit growth are borrowed from future loss absorption.

We value OK Bank with residual income and warranted price-to-book, the house method for banks. A bank's value is the book equity plus the present value of the spread between ROE and the cost of equity, so the method forces us to state the two numbers that matter: the sustainable return on equity and the discount rate. Multiples are a cross-check only; a small bank's earnings are too cyclical and its payout too thin for a PE-led valuation to be meaningful [S0].

The cost of equity build is in the table below. The engine uses a risk-free rate of 7.4%, less the Indonesian default spread of 1.6%, plus a beta of 0.90 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 11.9%. We use the unlevered beta because a bank is valued on the equity side only; gearing is inside the ROE, not in the discount rate. The total equity risk premium used is therefore about 4.2% plus 2.5%, slightly above the house's IDR band of five to six percent. We keep the deck number rather than shade it down because a higher discount rate lowers our value; the sell case does not depend on a generous cost of capital.

The primary method is the warranted P/BV identity. The sustainable ROE is 4.9%, the average of the FY2026E-FY2028E path — the level the bank reaches once the 2025-26 provisioning trough closes, and still far below the 11.9% cost of equity. With a cost of equity of 11.9% and terminal growth of 3.0%, the warranted multiple is 0.22x book, or Rp51 per share.

Growth and payout have to be reconciled here, and in most bank models they are not. The identity is that perpetual growth equals ROE times the retention ratio: one growth rate is only consistent with one payout. At a 4.9% sustainable ROE and 3.0% growth, the implied terminal payout is roughly two-fifths of earnings. Our explicit forecast pays nothing in any of the five years, because the bank has never paid a dividend, so the distribution is an assumption about the terminal year rather than a forecast we can source. The alternative treatment is the one a zero-payout purist would run: hold payout at zero forever, let book compound at ROE and set g equal to ROE. That collapses the warranted multiple to zero, because a bank that never distributes and earns less than its cost of equity is worth nothing to a minority holder beyond a control event. We do not use it — a bank with a 42.2% capital ratio and a float that has to be repaired cannot retain everything forever — but it is the reason the value is so sensitive to the terminal distribution, and it is why a genuine capital-return policy is the single largest re-rating lever in this name. The residual-income model, which discounts the actual yearly shortfall between profit and the cost of equity and then capitalises the terminal shortfall, produces Rp45. It is -10.6% below the primary method.

The divergence is informative rather than a problem. The P/BV identity uses an average sustainable ROE and assumes the bank can hold it; the residual-income model compounds a negative spread on a growing equity base, so it is more punitive when returns stay below the cost of equity for a long time. Neither method captures the option value of a sale of control or a capital return, which is why we do not push the target to the residual-income number alone. We weight the two methods equally, which gives Rp45. The scenario-weighted value, which gives partial credit to a better margin and a cleaner credit cycle, is Rp56; after the house liquidity discount for a 7.5% float and thin turnover, the twelve-month target is Rp45 [S0].

What does today's price imply? At 0.4x FY2026E book, the market is capitalising a sustainable ROE materially above the 4.3% the bank earned in FY2025 and above anything in our forecast. Our reverse-DCF engine cannot bracket the current price with any credit cost in the plausible range; in plain terms, the price is not a discount to a conservative value, it is a different view of the franchise. The market is either pricing a control event, a capital return, or a recovery in returns that the balance sheet has not produced in four years of data. We are not paid to assume the first two, and the third is contradicted by the margin and provisioning math.

A word on the multiple, because the wrong comparison would flatter the stock. At 0.42 times book, DNAR is not obviously expensive against the large Indonesian banks, which trade at one to two times book on double-digit returns; that comparison tells us nothing. The relevant comparator is the small-bank tier our desk covers, where sub-scale franchises earning below their cost of equity change hands at fractions of book for exactly the reason this model sets out. Against those names DNAR's multiple is not the anomaly — the ROE is. Working the identity backwards at today's 0.42 multiple, a 11.9% cost of equity and 3.0% growth implies a sustainable ROE of roughly six and three-quarter percent: about two and a half points above the 4.3% the bank earned in FY2025, and above every year in our forecast. The market is not pricing a discount to warranted book; it is pricing a franchise that the filings do not show.
The risks are real in both directions, and we set them out with likelihood and impact rather than as a list.

**Funding and liquidity (high likelihood, high impact).** An LDR of 119.5% against a system 88.1% is the bank's defining vulnerability [S0][S22]. If deposit growth slows — and system DPK growth is decelerating to 8.2%, with the central bank's own survey pointing lower — the bank must pay more for wholesale money or slow lending. Either outcome compresses NIM and ROE, and for a bank this size the adjustment is not a gentle one: there is no CASA franchise to lean on and no securities book to sell down. Our bear case runs that mechanism explicitly: deposits grow four percentage points slower than base, NIM gives up forty basis points permanently and loan growth is cut four points to keep the LDR from rising further. A policy-rate rise toward 6.2% would make it worse, because deposit costs reprice faster than corporate assets [S20], and that is the second half of the same shock.

**Credit-cost normalisation (high likelihood, high impact).** The FY2025 profit jump came largely from a lower provision charge, and 2026 provisioning is running near zero [S0]. A return to a through-cycle cost of risk removes a large part of the current earnings base. We cannot size the company's own tail because its NPL, LAR and coverage ratios are not in any source we could archive. We can size the system: gross NPL of 2.1% and a loan-at-risk ratio of 8.5% [S22] mean the banking system still carries a meaningful stock of stressed credit even at this point in the cycle, and a small corporate lender without a disclosed asset-quality record should be assumed to be at least at the system's risk, not below it. That is why the base case normalises the charge to 1.2% and the bear adds another forty basis points on top.

**Capital and payout (medium likelihood, high impact).** 42.2% CAR is a cushion but also a drag: with no dividend, the bank keeps compounding equity at a low return [S16][S0]. The size of the trapped capital is the point. Against the system's 24.3% capital ratio, the equity above that benchmark is roughly two-fifths of the IDR4,006.8bn of forecast FY2026E equity, because the bank runs at roughly 39.5% and lends only 117.9% of its deposits. Per share, that excess is a similar share of the Rp237 book value — close to the entire IDR1,689.2bn the market currently pays for the company. A special dividend or buyback of that capital would transfer book value to shareholders at par, and at a 0.42 multiple a buyback would be mechanically accretive to book value per share for those who remain. We nonetheless carry it at zero weight in the target: a buyback shrinks a 7.5% float that already breaches the exchange's 15.0% minimum [S24], and a special dividend is a discretionary decision of a controlling shareholder who has chosen retention for every year in the data history [S0]. It is the catalyst that would change the rating fastest, not a base-case assumption.

**Governance and free float (medium likelihood, high impact).** Insiders own 91.4% and the float is 7.5% against the exchange's 15.0% minimum [S0][S24]. A rights issue to fix the float would dilute minorities at a low price; a sell-down could improve liquidity but also pressure the shares. Related-party flows with the Korean parent are not quantified in our sources [S2], and we have not found a current annual report that would let us size them. We therefore state plainly that the governance and dilution tail — a discounted rights issue, a related-party loss, a transfer of value to the parent — is unquantified and excluded from the bear value. The bear is a credit-and-funding path; it is not a governance path, and a governance event would take the value below it.

**Liquidity and exit (high likelihood, medium impact).** Average daily turnover of IDR140.2m means a modest position cannot be exited quickly [S0]. This is why the target carries a 20% discount; it is also why the shares can stay mispriced for longer than a fundamental investor can stay solvent.

**Macro and currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The rupiah is at 18,228 against the dollar and the house deck expects 18,350 [S0]. A disorderly depreciation would force BI to tighten further, squeezing the margin and slowing credit. The bank has no direct commodity exposure, so this is a second-order risk transmitted through rates.

Our bear case (probability 30.0%) is the funding squeeze: deposits grow three percentage points slower than base, NIM gives up forty basis points, credit growth is cut four points and credit cost runs forty basis points above base. It values the shares at Rp5. That number is severe, and it should be read for what it is. The warranted value of this bank is the capitalised spread between a mid-single-digit ROE and an 11.9% cost of equity; when a forty-basis-point NIM shock removes most of that spread, the going-concern value collapses toward zero even though book equity and the 42.2% capital ratio are intact. It is a value of the franchise, not of the balance sheet, and it excludes any control or liquidation value of the capital. The base case (45.0%) is the model above, at Rp48. The bull case (25.0%) assumes the CASA strategy works — deposits three points above base, a forty-basis-point NIM improvement, credit four points above base and a credit charge down to ten basis points — and it values the shares at Rp108. The probabilities put two-thirds of the weight on the bear and base paths, because the funding arithmetic and the provisioning trough are observed facts rather than risks; the bull case is what happens if management's CASA plan works and asset quality holds. Today's price sits between our base and bull values, which is the cleanest statement of the disagreement.

Signposts that would change our view: a decisive fall in the LDR toward the system average without a margin collapse; a credit charge that stays well below one percent for four consecutive quarters with disclosure that supports it; a capital-return announcement at the AGM; a free-float remedy that brings in a strategic investor at a premium; and any evidence that the Korean parent is prepared to inject capital at a price above book. Conversely, a rising LDR, a jump in loan-at-risk or a discounted rights issue would confirm the bear case.

Ownership is concentrated and the minority is small. Insiders hold 91.4%, institutions hold 0.0% and the free float is 7.5% on the data pack's IDX-IC ownership-registry mirror [S0], against the exchange's 15.0% minimum for continued listing [S24]. The controlling shareholder is a Korean financial group: APRO Financial Co Ltd took its stake above ninety percent in the 2022 rights issue at an exercise price far above today's market [S2], and the data pack names OK Next Co Ltd as the parent [S0]. We could not reconcile the two from primary documents, and we treat the discrepancy as a disclosure gap. There are no pledged-share disclosures in our sources; we flag the absence rather than assert that no pledge exists.

The board and management are Korean-led. The president director is Bong Joo Kang; the compliance director and corporate secretary is Efdinal Alamsyah; the deputy president director who presented the FY2025 results is Hendra Lie [S0][S16]. The combination of a controlling Korean parent and a Korean-led board is not a governance problem in itself, but it does mean that related-party transactions, capital injections and dividend policy are decided by the parent, not by the minority. We could not obtain a current annual report, so the auditor, the audit opinion and the related-party note are unverified. That is a genuine gap in a name where governance is a material part of the discount, and we report it as such.

The dividend record is empty: no dividend in any year of the data history, and a trailing yield of 0.0% [S0]. The October 2025 treasury-share cancellation reduced the share count to 16,892 million and was approved at an extraordinary general meeting [S3]. It is a capital-structure clean-up, not a return of capital, and it raises the insider percentage because the denominator fell.

ESG exposures are modest and mostly governance-related. The bank has no coal, palm-oil or mining exposure, so the climate transition is not a direct earnings risk. Its social contribution is financial inclusion and MSME lending, and the system's MSME credit growth running at a low single-digit rate suggests that segment is not where the growth is [S22]. The material ESG issue is data privacy and cyber risk from the digital onboarding and mobile-banking push [S16]; for a bank of this size, a cyber incident would be an operational and reputational event, not just a compliance one. Governance dominates the ESG discount: concentration, float, disclosure and related-party opacity are the things we would need to see fixed before paying more than warranted book.

The near-term calendar is thin, which is itself part of the problem for an illiquid name. The FY2026 audited results, expected around March 2027, are the next hard information point: we will look at whether the near-zero 2026 provisioning charge survives the audit, and at the LDR and NIM trajectory. The annual general meeting, expected around May 2027, is the forum for any capital-return or free-float remedy. Bank Indonesia's board meetings are the macro swing factor, with the market projecting a policy rate near 6.2% by year-end 2026 [S20]. Any announcement on the free float — a rights issue, a private placement or a strategic sale — would be the single largest re-rating event, in either direction [S0].

Between updates we monitor six KPIs. NIM and cost of funds, because the spread is the whole business. The LDR, because it tells us whether growth is being funded prudently. CASA composition, because it is management's stated fix for the funding cost. Credit cost and loan-at-risk, because the last two years of profit depend on a benign charge. CAR and RWA density, because the capital cushion is both the strength and the drag. And the free float, because the structural overhang is the difference between a value trap and a re-rating candidate. None of these is currently moving in a direction that would make us pay today's price [S0][S16].

bear.narrative: A funding squeeze: deposit growth stalls 3pp below base as system DPK deceleration bites, the bank pays up for wholesale money and NIM falls 40bp, credit growth is cut 4pp to protect liquidity, and credit cost runs 40bp above base as the 2025-26 provisioning trough normalises

bull.narrative: The CASA strategy works: deposits grow 3pp above base and the cheaper mix lifts NIM 40bp, credit grows 4pp above base into selective corporate assets, and the credit charge falls to 10bp as asset quality holds rather than turning negative

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the latest actual, not on guidance: loans were Rp10.81tn in May 2026, up 12.66% yoy from Rp9.60tn, and Rp10.73tn at Dec-2025, up 15.4% from Rp9.30tn in FY2024 [S19][S16]. FY2026E therefore holds the latest yoy rate at 12.5%, in line with system credit growth of 13.26% [S22]. Growth then steps down to 11% and 10% because the 119% loan-to-deposit ratio ties lending to deposit gathering, and converges to 10% long run, below system credit growth

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the actuals: DPK grew 19.1% in FY2025 to Rp8,98tn from Rp7,54tn [S16] and was up 28.86% yoy at May-2026, though the May level of Rp8,54tn is below the Rp8,98tn December print because deposits run off in the first half [S19]. FY2026E assumes 14%, which requires a strong second half but keeps deposits ahead of 12.5% loan growth and takes the 119% loan-to-deposit ratio toward the system's 88.11% [S22]; the pace then converges to 11.5% long run as the CASA strategy matures

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Earning assets are proxied by total assets, the house convention for this template and the same denominator the NIM input is measured on: Rp13,42tn of total assets against Rp10,73tn of loans is 1.25x at FY2025 [S16], 1.28x at FY2024 (Rp11,87tn / Rp9,30tn) [S16], with total assets at Rp14,19tn by 2026Q3 [S0]. Held at 1.25x, so forecast earning assets and forecast total assets carry the same loan-driven growth

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Measured on average total assets, the template's denominator: FY2025A NII of Rp688,88bn on average assets of Rp12,64tn is 5.45% [S16], and nine-month 2026 NII of Rp606,3bn annualises to Rp808bn on average assets of Rp13,80tn, or 5.86% [S0]. FY2026E holds the 9M run-rate at 5.85%; the base then gives back 15bp to 5.70% long run as system deposit growth of 8.22% trails credit growth of 13.26% [S22] and the bank pays up for term money. The house macro deck holds BI at 5.75% through FY2027E, so there is no policy-rate compression in this path

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Non-interest income is a rounding error (0.7% of FY2025A total operating income) and volatile; held flat in money terms rather than extrapolating the negative FY2023A base [S16]

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025A cost-to-income is about 60% once operating expenses are derived from pre-provision profit [S0]; digital-channel investment is offset by branch optimisation, so held at 60% rather than improved

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: Through-cycle cost of risk, not the near-zero 9M2026 charge: FY2024A implied provisioning was about 1.9% of loans before FY2025A fell to about 0.65% [S0]; 0.5% in FY2026E allows a modest Q4 catch-up on the 9M run-rate, then normalises to 1.2% by FY2029E

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Minorities share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid in any year of the data history (S0) and the bank is still accumulating capital; 0% assumed throughout, which makes the DDM method inapplicable and is reflected in the valuation weights

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Implied from the disclosed 42.21% CAR [S16] and equity of Rp3,797bn on Rp10,730bn loans: RWA/loans = 3,797/(0.4221 x 10,730) = 0.84x; held constant

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 3.0%, below the house IDR terminal-growth cap and below nominal GDP. The identity g = ROE x (1 - payout) is applied explicitly: at the engine's sustainable ROE, which is the average of the FY2026E-FY2028E path, 3.0% implies a terminal payout of about two-fifths of earnings, against the zero payout of the five explicit years. The alternative treatment - payout stays at zero forever, so book compounds at ROE and g = ROE - collapses the warranted multiple to zero, which is why the terminal year, not the forecast, carries the distribution assumption

challenges.challenge: The loan-growth basis asserts the company's 9.5% target and the deposit basis asserts a company 10% DPK guide, both citing [S19], but the archived S19 contains only 28.86% DPK growth, 12.66% loan growth, a 6.18% BI survey DPK forecast and a 13.83% 2025 DPK outcome - no 9.5% or 10% company guidance. These uncited figures are load-bearing for the 6% loan-growth haircut and the 10% deposit path.
challenges.answer: Dropped both guidance claims: no archived source contains a 9.5% loan target or a 10% DPK guide, so neither is cited or used. Loan growth is now rebuilt from the May-2026 actual of +12.66% yoy (F32, S19) and system credit growth of 13.26% (F16, S22); deposit growth from FY2025's +19.1% (F2/F4, S16) and the May-2026 +28.86% yoy print (S19). The Rp10.81tn May level versus Rp10.73tn in December is treated as first-half deposit seasonality, not annualised.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E loan growth is set at 6.0% (loans 10,730 to 11,373.8) while the latest actual is +12.66% YoY to Rp10.81tn in May-2026 [S19] and system credit grew 13.26% [S22]. The only support is Dec-2025 to May-2026 growth of +0.7%, a seasonally weak five-month window that the same article reports as +12.66% YoY. This is a below-actual volume haircut without a sourced reason.
challenges.answer: FY2026E loan growth raised from 6.0% to 12.5%, in line with the latest actual of +12.66% yoy to Rp10.81tn in May-2026 (S19) and system credit growth of 13.26% (S22). The five-month Dec-May stub is no longer used as the primary signal; the report states why it is seasonal and does not annualise it. Growth then steps to 11% and 10% on the LDR constraint, not as a precautionary haircut.

challenges.challenge: Warranted P/BV uses g = 3.0% and sustainable ROE = 4.5% with payout = 0%. The identity requires g = ROE x (1 - payout); 3% implies a ~33% payout that the forecast does not make, and the RI terminal capitalises the final shortfall at 3% while book equity compounds at ~4.4%. Both choices raise the value versus a consistent zero-payout treatment and are not reconciled.
challenges.answer: The growth/payout identity is now explicit: sustainable ROE is the engine's FY2026E-FY2028E average of 4.91%, and at 3.0% terminal growth that implies a terminal payout of about two-fifths of earnings, against zero payout in the five explicit years. Section 4 also shows the zero-payout treatment - book compounding at ROE with g equal to ROE - which collapses the warranted multiple to zero, and explains why it is not used.

challenges.challenge: The ea_loans basis is internally unreproducible: Rp705.8bn at the disclosed 5.67% NIM implies average earning assets near Rp12.45tn, or 1.16x the Rp10.73tn loan book, but the input sets 1.22x (Rp13.09tn) and the FY2025A model earning-asset line is total assets of Rp13.42tn (1.25x). Three different denominators feed the NII forecast.
challenges.answer: ea_loans was restated to 1.25x, the ratio of the denominator actually used (total assets Rp13.42tn over loans Rp10.73tn at FY2025, S16), and NIM was re-measured on that same average-total-assets basis: 5.45% for FY2025 (filed NII Rp688.88bn) and 5.86% for 9M2026 (Rp606.3bn annualised on Rp13.8tn). The old 5.67%/1.22x mix is gone and section 3 now carries an explicit NII bridge from the filed figure to the FY2026E forecast.

challenges.challenge: FY2025A net interest income is Rp705.76bn in the model (pack S0) but Rp688.88bn in the source [S16, F14], a Rp16.88bn (2.4%) gap that no justification reconciles. Section 1 then pairs NII of Rp688.9bn with 'total operating income of roughly Rp705.8bn', which arithmetically gives Rp694.2bn, not Rp705.8bn.
challenges.answer: Section 1 no longer pairs the filed NII with the pack's total operating income: it now states the company's Rp688.88bn (F14, S16), the pack's Rp705.76bn interest line, non-interest income of Rp5.31bn and total operating income of Rp711.06bn, which add. Section 3 explains the Rp16.9bn difference as the pack deriving interest income less interest expense (Rp1,206.7bn less Rp501.0bn) rather than the LK's net interest line, and shows it does not touch np, equity or ROE.

challenges.challenge: The base case compresses NIM from a 5.9% 9M2026 run-rate to 5.5% by FY2029E, justified partly by a possible BI rate rise to 6.00-6.25% from one economist [S20]. The house macro deck carries BI at 5.75% for both spot and FY2027E, i.e. flat, and the engine does not read the deck rate. The base therefore assumes a rate path the firm does not forecast.
challenges.answer: The base case no longer embeds a policy-rate rise. NIM is held at the 9M2026 run-rate of 5.85% and drifts only to 5.70% long run on deposit competition, with the house macro deck's flat 5.75% BI path stated in the text; the hike toward 6.25% (S20) is now carried only in the bear case and the risk section.

challenges.challenge: The text says the 0.4x multiple implies a sustainable ROE 'several points above anything the bank has delivered'. At 0.42x FY2026E book, COE 11.85% and g 3%, the implied sustainable ROE is about 6.7% - roughly 2.4pp above the 4.3% FY2025 ROE, not several points. The 'Indonesian banks that trade at one to two times book' comparison ignores the house small-bank peer set at 0.26-0.52x (BACA, BKSW, BBTN, BJTM), several of them BUY.
challenges.answer: The implied-ROE arithmetic is now stated: at 0.42x FY2026E book, a 11.85% cost of equity and 3.0% growth, today's price implies a sustainable ROE of about 6.7%, roughly two and a half points above the 4.30% earned in FY2025 - not several points. The large-cap one-to-two-times-book comparison is removed and replaced with the small-bank tier, where fractions of book are the norm; the SELL is retained on that corrected comparison.

challenges.challenge: The report names a genuine capital-return policy as the first thing that could change the view, but the bull scenario contains only credit-cost, NIM and loan-growth shocks. With 42.2% CAR and a 0.44x multiple, a buyback or special dividend is mechanically accretive to BVPS and ROE and is the most plausible value-transfer catalyst; it is not modelled or probability-weighted anywhere.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now quantifies the capital-return option: against the system's 24.3% CAR (S22), the capital above that benchmark is about two-fifths of forecast FY2026E equity, a similar share of book value per share and close to the entire market capitalisation. A buyback at 0.42x would be accretive to remaining holders. It carries zero weight in the target because a buyback would shrink a 7.53% float that already breaches the 15% minimum (S24) and a special dividend is the controlling shareholder's discretionary call after a zero-dividend history (S0).

challenges.challenge: The base credits none of the observed funding improvement: DPK grew 28.86% YoY to Rp8.54tn in May-2026 [S19] and system giro grew 12.64% [S18], exactly management's CASA strategy, yet deposits are assumed to grow 10% and NIM to fall to 5.5% from the 5.9% 9M2026 run-rate. A faster CASA mix lowering cost of funds is the obvious upside case and is absent.
challenges.answer: The CASA-led improvement is now the bull case, not a missing upside: the bull lifts deposit growth three points above base and NIM forty basis points, and the report links that to the observed 28.86% yoy DPK growth (S19) and 12.64% system giro growth (S18). The base still assumes 14% deposit growth, because the May level of Rp8.54tn is below the December Rp8.98tn print and the full-year path needs a strong second half.

challenges.challenge: The bear case has no discounted rights issue, free-float remedy or related-party loss, although section 5 says a float-fixing rights issue 'would dilute minorities at a low price'. The 60bp credit-cost shock is also unanchored: the company's own NPL/LAR/coverage is not in the facts, and the 8.5% system LAR [S22] is not used to size a tail.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries a funding shock set - deposits -3pp, NIM -40bp, loan growth -4pp, credit cost +40bp - rather than a single unanchored credit number, and the credit cost is anchored to system gross NPL of 2.07% and LAR of 8.5% (S22). On the governance tail we state plainly that a discounted rights issue, a related-party loss or a transfer to the parent is unquantified and excluded from the bear value, because no current annual report or related-party note could be archived.

challenges.challenge: The calibration justification describes Rp705.8bn as the 'model forecast' and the forecast NIM as 5.6%, but 705.8 is the FY2025A pack line and the FY2026E NIM input is 5.9%; the 0.88pp FY2025A (4.30%) to FY2026E (5.18%) ROE gap is not explained. The QC output also lists calibration and drift as orphan justifications.
challenges.answer: The orphan calibration and drift justifications were deleted. The FY2025 4.30% to FY2026E 5.37% ROE step is now explained in section 3 as the arithmetic of a 5.85% margin on 12.5% asset growth with a near-zero provision charge, reversing as the charge normalises, and the Rp705.8bn versus Rp688.9bn NII difference is explained as a pack presentation line, not a profit restatement.

challenges.challenge: The mirrored bull shock subtracts 0.6pp from a 0.5% base credit cost, leaving -0.1%, i.e. a net provisioning write-back, while the bull narrative says asset quality 'stays clean' (zero, not negative). This inflates the bull value that feeds the probability-weighted target.
challenges.answer: The bull credit shock was cut from -0.6pp to -0.4pp, so bull credit cost is 0.1% rather than -0.1%: no provisioning write-back is assumed and the bull narrative says the charge falls to ten basis points, not below zero. Bear and bull shocks are now equal and opposite on all four drivers.

challenges.challenge: The 7.53% free float is cited [S0], but the datapack's free_float_source is the IDX-IC registry mirror dated 2026-11-04, and neither S0 nor any cited source states the 15% threshold the report invokes. The 'clean-looking loan book' in the summary also has no company NPL, LAR or coverage figure behind it.
challenges.answer: The float is now cited to the data pack's IDX-IC ownership-registry mirror (S0) and the 15% threshold to the exchange rule archived as S24, with a new fact F31. The unsourced 'clean-looking loan book' is removed from the investment summary, which now states that the company's NPL, LAR and coverage ratios are not in any archived source.

challenges.challenge: The funding risk is rated high likelihood/high impact in the prose, but the bear scenario sizes it only as a 40bp NIM squeeze. With LDR at 119.5% and system DPK growth decelerating to 8.22% (and BI survey 6.18% for 2026) [S18][S19], a deposit stall would force wholesale funding at a much larger cost increase or a sudden loan-book contraction - neither is modelled, so the bear understates the bank's defining vulnerability.
challenges.answer: The bear is now a funding squeeze rather than a 40bp NIM trim: deposit growth falls three points below base, NIM loses 40bp, loan growth is cut four points and credit cost rises 40bp. Section 5 explains why a 119.5% LDR bank cannot absorb this gently - no CASA franchise and no securities book to sell - and shows the LDR path easing only slowly under the base case as deposits outgrow loans.

missing_bull_case.note: No capital-return, buyback or control-sale scenario despite 42.2% CAR, 0.44x book and the report itself calling a buyback the first thing that could change the view; the bull case varies only credit cost, NIM and loan growth.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear scenario has no discounted rights issue, free-float remedy dilution or related-party loss, even though the report says a float-fixing rights issue would dilute minorities at a low price; the 60bp credit shock is not anchored to the company's LAR or the 8.5% system LAR.

assumption_realism.note: The ea_loans basis is not reproducible: 705.8bn at 5.67% implies ~12.45tn (1.16x loans), the input is 1.22x (13.09tn) and FY2025A model earning assets are total assets 13.42tn (1.25x); the deposit 10% is labelled company guidance but S19 only gives a 6.18% BI survey.

evidence_and_citations.note: The 9.5% loan-growth target and the 10% DPK company guide are both attributed to S19, which contains neither; free float is cited to S0 although the datapack source is the IDX-IC registry; the 'one to two times book' peer claim is uncited and contradicted by the house small-bank peer set.

valuation_method_fit.note: Terminal g of 3% with 4.5% sustainable ROE and a 0% payout violates g = ROE x (1 - payout) and implies a 33% payout the model does not have; the RI terminal grows at 3% while book compounds at ~4.4%. The method is right for a bank but the growth/payout pair is inconsistent.

bias_and_tone.note: At 0.42x FY2026E book, 11.85% COE and 3% g the implied market ROE is ~6.7%, about 2.4pp above the 4.3% earned - not 'several points' above anything delivered; the 'one to two times book' comparison ignores the relevant small-bank peers at 0.26-0.52x.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Base NIM compression to 5.5% relies on a possible BI rise to 6.00-6.25% from an external economist [S20], while the house macro deck carries BI at 5.75% spot and FY2027E, i.e. flat; the model does not read the deck rate.

conservatism_audit.note: FY2026E loan growth of 6% is below the latest actual +12.66% YoY [S19] and below system 13.26% [S22], on a seasonal Dec-to-May +0.7% comparison; NIM falls from a 5.9% 9M2026 run-rate to 5.5% against a flat deck rate; terminal g is below sustainable growth. Each drift is unsourced.

calibration.note: qc_justifications.calibration calls Rp705.8bn the 'model forecast' and the forecast NIM 5.6% (the input is 5.9%); it does not explain the 0.88pp FY2025A-to-FY2026E ROE gap, and calibration/drift are listed as orphan justifications.

signoff.notes: Initiation passes the house bar. Evidence: check PASS (facts + lint), engine QC clear, 14 red-team answers each leave a visible trace in the report and the model - FY2026E loan growth rebuilt at 12.5% in the inputs and in section 3 off the May-2026 actual and system credit 13.3% [S19][S22]; NIM held at 5.85% with BI flat on the house deck [S20]; pack-vs-filed NII difference (705.8 vs 688.9) explained as presentation netting with profit, equity and ROE unaffected [S0][S16]; payout/g reconciled with the zero-payout alternative shown; bull credit cost floored at 10bp; funding bear explicit (deposits -3pp, NIM -40bp, loans -4pp); governance/dilution tail stated as unquantified and excluded from bear value; capital-return catalyst carried at zero weight with the 7.53% float vs 15% minimum [S24] and retention history as the reason. Base case is most-likely, not cautious: scenario-weighted value 56.1 exceeds the 47.96 method blend and the 25% bull weight carries 2.2x base value, so the distribution is not lopsided to the downside; the QC too-bearish note (~14% harsh) was quantified and answered. Batch bias check: BANKS batch is mixed (BUY BBRI/BBYB/BJTM/BNGA/BTPS vs SELL BACA/BCIC/BGTG/BNBA); DNAR's SELL rests on its own 4.35% FY2025 ROE and 119.5% LDR, not a shared input. Two cosmetic defects for next touch, neither rating-moving: (1) section 4 says weighting P/BV 51 and RI 45 equally gives Rp45 - the equal-weight blend is Rp48, Rp45 is the 20% liquidity discount on the Rp56 scenario-weighted TP and the next sentence derives it correctly; (2) section 5 funding-risk prose says bear deposits run four points slower than base while the modelled shock and scenario narrative use 3pp. Multiple-method warning accepted: DDM weight moved to RI with a sourced zero-payout reason.

bias.note: Mild but quantified. The 50%-weighted primary method capitalises a 4.91% ROE - the FY2026E-FY2028E average - while the model's own ROE falls to 4.64% in FY2028E, bottoms at 4.57% in FY2029E and reaches 6.08% by FY2035E; at 6.08% with COE 11.85% and g 3% the warranted multiple is 0.35x (Rp82), the blend Rp63 and the target about Rp51, so the -55% is roughly 14% too harsh. Offsetting: the RI cross-check independently gives 45.3 on the full ROE path, the 30% bear weight is defensible given LDR 119.5% and a near-zero 9M2026 charge, and the rating survives the correction. Not too_bullish on any driver - loan growth 12.5% vs 12.66% actual [S19], NIM 5.85% vs 5.86% 9M run-rate [S0], deposit growth 14% below the 19.1% FY2025 actual [S16].

findings.finding: fund record:112 and fund record:210-213 describe the 4.91% sustainable ROE (engine default = FY2026E-FY2028E average) as the level reached once the provisioning trough closes, but ROE is 4.72% in FY2027E, 4.64% in FY2028E and bottoms at 4.57% in FY2029E, reaching 6.08% only by FY2035E. The perpetuity is capitalised on a transitional average, not the through-cycle return.

fund record:34 and fund record:116 both render the method blend as Rp45. The equal-weight blend of 50.65 and 45.27 is Rp47.96, and the packet prints method blend today 48; Rp45 is the target after scenario weighting (56) and the 20% liquidity discount. Section 4 later contradicts these sentences.

fund record:92 says the margin holds at 5.85% and that this takes NII from the filed Rp688.88bn to Rp833.89bn. The model's FY2025A NII is the pack's 705.76 (nim_line 5.58%); a held 5.85% on the filed 688.88 implies about Rp787bn. On the filed basis the margin rises 40bp, it does not hold. This repeats the two-basis NII error the red team raised as C5.

fund record:130 says the bear has deposits growing four percentage points slower than base; the model shock is a.deposit_growth -0.03 and fund record:140 says three points. The section contradicts itself and the table.
fund record:90 says deposits grow 14.0% in FY2026E, more than in FY2025 on our numbers. FY2025 DPK grew 19.1% (8,980 from 7,540, F2/F4 [S16]); 14% is a 5pp deceleration, not an acceleration.

Section 6 (fund record:148-160) covers ownership, float, board and ESG but never states DNAR's IDX board or any notation letters, which the banks method card lists in its output contract and which matters for a 7.5% float name under free-float pressure.

The extreme_call justification at fund record:259 asserts the 119.5% LDR pays the system's highest funding cost. No archived source ranks DNAR's cost of funds; S16 gives the LDR only. The load-bearing drivers (ROE 4.35%, CAR 42.21%, LDR 119.5%, 7.53% float) are each sourced, so the flag itself stands.

The post_bs_review note (fund record:218) lists only the October-2025 treasury cancellation; a 20 May 2026 Bisnis report has OK Bank setting out a strategy to lift the free float, a post-balance-sheet statement on the structural risk section 5 already flags.

flags.message: expected return -55%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The minus-sixty-percent expected return is driven by three sourced facts, not by a cautious forecast: FY2025 ROE of 4.35% on a 42.21% CAR [S16], so equity compounds faster than the bank can deploy it at its own cost of equity; a loan-to-deposit ratio of 119.5% (loans Rp10.73tn against DPK Rp8.98tn) [S16] that forces deposit-led growth and pays the system's highest funding cost; and a 7.53% free float against the exchange's 15% minimum [S0][S24]. Today's 0.42x book implies a sustainable ROE of roughly 6.7%, against 4.35% earned in FY2025 and a forecast path averaging 4.9%: the price needs a franchise the filings do not show.
